title: Perceptual CIELAB Brick Mosaic & 3D Stud Relief

cells.source:
# Perceptual CIELAB Brick Mosaic & 3D Stud Relief

Brick-art mosaic kits turn a picture into a board of round studs in a handful of plastic colours. Three ideas make that work:

1. **Match colours the way eyes do.** Measuring the gap between two colours by their red, green and blue numbers misjudges what people see, because we notice some differences far more than others. The **CIELAB** colour space is built so that equal distances look about equally different; the distance is called **ΔE**, and a ΔE of about 2 is the smallest most people can spot.
2. **Spread the error**, known as *Floyd–Steinberg dithering*. Each stud's colour is a little off; pass that error on to the studs not yet chosen (7⁄16 to the right, and 3⁄16, 5⁄16 and 1⁄16 below), and from a distance the eye blends the speckle into colours the palette doesn't have.
3. **Add depth.** Stacking 1 to 4 plates under the brighter parts turns a flat board into a relief.

C turns three artworks into 28 × 28 mosaics from 12 brick colours, and measures how far each is from the original, both close up and from a distance. A picture compares them, and three.js builds the relief.

How the cells run:

- **C runs in your browser.** The cell is compiled to WebAssembly by xcc, on the page, and runs at once, on the website too.
- **C reads the controls with `nb_get_int` and `nb_get_number`.** After changing the artwork, metric or dithering, press **▶** on the C cell; the relief slider works straight away.

> ✨ The code cells were written by an AI model from prompts, and each prompt is saved in its cell: press **✨** in a cell's header to see it.

Press **Run all**.

## 2. Make the mosaic in C

> In C, turn a picture into a 28 × 28 brick mosaic in 12 brick colours. Read the artwork (mosaic_scene: 0 a great wave and a red sun, 1 an aurora over mountains, 2 a spiral galaxy), the colour metric (mosaic_metric: 1 CIELAB, 0 plain RGB) and the dithering strength from nb with <nb.h>. Draw each artwork from formulas, with a relief height of 1 to 4 plates per stud. Convert colours from sRGB to CIELAB, through linear RGB and XYZ (D65). Choose each stud's colour as the nearest by the chosen metric, and pass its RGB error, times the dithering strength, on to the unvisited neighbours with Floyd–Steinberg weights. Measure the colour error against the original artwork two ways: each stud's ΔE, and each 3 × 3 patch's ΔE with its light averaged in linear RGB, as seen from a distance. Print both and the studs of each colour, and share nb.mosaic_art with the palette, each stud's colour and height, the two errors, and the artwork.

- **`rgb_to_lab`** undoes the screen's brightness curve (`srgb_to_lin`), mixes the light into XYZ, then bends it into CIELAB with a cube root, roughly how our eyes respond.
- **The dithering loop** visits studs left to right, top to bottom, so the error only ever goes to studs not yet chosen. `dither` scales how much is passed on: 0 is none at all.
- **`stud_de` and `patch_de`** are the two errors. Both compare against `origR`, `origG` and `origB`, the artwork before any error was passed around.

## 4. Close up and from a distance

> Show three pictures side by side on canvases, 9 pixels per stud: the artwork in nb.mosaic_art, the brick mosaic as round studs in their brick colours on a dark board, and the mosaic as seen from a distance, each stud replaced by the average light (in linear RGB) of its 3 × 3 patch. Under them, captions with the close-up and from-a-distance colour errors. Redraw whenever nb changes. Dark theme.

The middle picture is what you'd see with your nose to the board; the right one is roughly what you'd see from across the room. Turn the dithering off and run the C cell again to see what it was doing.

## What the run shows

- **The wave uses 9 of the 12 colours.** Its dusk sky, lavender fading to sand, has no match in the palette, so most of it becomes light bluish grey: 280 of the 784 studs.
- **Dithering trades close up for far away.** At 75%, the default, each stud is ΔE 14.6 from the artwork, but 3 × 3 patches are only 6.5 off. With no dithering, studs are closer (12.2), but patches are 10.3 off and the sea turns into bands. Full strength buys almost nothing more from afar (6.4) and costs a lot close up (18.1).
- **CIELAB beats plain RGB.** Close up, it's closer for every artwork: 14.6 against 16.0 for the wave, 17.5 against 19.7 for the aurora, and 29.5 against 36.7 for the galaxy. From a distance it wins on the wave (6.5 against 9.0) and by far on the galaxy (16.9 against 33.3), and ties on the aurora (9.0).
- **The galaxy is the hardest.** Its purples and deep reds aren't in the palette, so even at best it's ΔE 16.9 off from afar, and there, full dithering makes it worse (18.1).

## Try this

Each of these is a prompt. Press **✨** in a cell's header to change its prompt and generate it again, or **⚡ AI Generate New Cell** at the bottom to add a new one.

- **Dithering off.** Set **Dithering Strength** to 0 and press **▶** on the C cell. The middle picture gets cleaner and the right one gets worse: smooth skies turn into bands.
- **More colours.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Add Dark Red, Medium Lavender, Sand Green and Reddish Brown to the palette."* Which artwork improves most?
- **Your own picture.** Press ✨ on the C cell and add: *"Add a fourth artwork: a sunset over a calm sea with a sailing boat."* Then press ✨ on the controls to add it to the list.
- **Understand the code.** Press the speech bubble (**Explain this cell**) on the C cell and ask why the error is passed only to studs that haven't been chosen yet.
